mainTopic: נדרים on cooked food: how vow words follow people's speech, רבי יאשיה on roasted food, and אביי's definition of תבשיל as food eaten with bread
overview: The משנה teaches that a נדר follows how people normally use words. Someone who vows off 'cooked food' may still eat roasted or well-boiled food. A vow on a 'תבשיל' covers loose pot dishes but not thick ones, and a vow on 'pot food' covers only boiled food, while 'whatever goes into a pot' covers everything cooked in a pot. A ברייתא says רבי יאשיה forbids roasted food too, hinting to this from a פסוק that calls the roasted קרבן פסח 'cooked.' The גמרא concludes that everyone agrees vows follow people's language: in רבי יאשיה's area people simply called roasted food 'cooked,' and the פסוק is only an אסמכתא. Then אביי explains that the משנה's תנא calls 'תבשיל' only food eaten with bread, and a ברייתא about soft gourds that the sick eat with bread supports him. The גמרא challenges this with a story of a doctor who called a gourd an 'angel of death' for a sick man. It gives three answers: soft versus hard gourds, the gourd itself versus its inside, or the 'sick' being weakened רבנן. The amud ends as the גמרא begins to show that רבא is consistent with another statement of his, which comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Vowing off cooked food still allows roasted and boiled food
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that someone who vows off מבושל may still eat צלי and שלוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone vows not to eat cooked food, he may still eat roasted food and food that was boiled for a long time.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens with a basic case: a person vows off 'cooked food.' It rules that roasted and heavily boiled foods are still allowed to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In everyday speech, people do not call roasted or long-boiled food 'cooked.' Each of these has its own name. So the vow only covers what people normally mean by the word מבושל.

keyTerms.meaning: Food boiled for a long time

phrases.english: One who vows off cooked food
is permitted to eat roasted and boiled food.
phrases.notes: שלוק means food boiled very thoroughly, so it has its own name and is not plain 'cooked.'

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow on מבושל does not include צלי or שלוק.

steps.title: Vowing off a cooked dish covers loose dishes only
steps.stepSummary: Someone who says 'קונם תבשיל' is forbidden in loose pot dishes but allowed thick ones, and also the special egg and gourd.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said, 'A cooked dish is קונם for me, I won't taste it,' he may not eat a soft or loose pot dish. He may eat a thick one, and he may also eat a ביצה טורמוטא and a דלעת הרמוצה.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to a slightly different wording, 'תבשיל,' and explains which foods that word covers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word תבשיל in normal speech means a loose dish made in a pot. A thick dish and the specially prepared egg and gourd are not called תבשיל, so they stay permitted. Again, the vow follows the way people actually talk.

keyTerms.meaning: A vow word that makes something forbidden like a קרבן

phrases.english: If he said: "A cooked dish is konam for me, that I will not taste"
he is forbidden to eat a loose pot dish,
and permitted to eat a thick one,
and permitted to eat a turemuta egg
and the remutza gourd.
phrases.notes: These are foods prepared in special ways, so people don't call them a תבשיל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new vow wording with its own range of forbidden foods
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow on תבשיל forbids loose pot dishes but not thick ones or the special egg and gourd.

steps.title: Pot food versus whatever goes into a pot
steps.stepSummary: A vow on מעשה קדרה forbids only boiled pot food, but a vow on 'what goes down into a pot' forbids everything cooked in a pot.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone vows off pot food, he is forbidden only food boiled in the pot. If he said, 'Whatever goes down into a pot is קונם, I won't taste it,' he is forbidden everything cooked in a pot.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה compares two pot-related wordings and shows that a broader wording creates a broader vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Pot food' is understood to mean food actually boiled in the pot. 'Whatever goes down into a pot' is wider and includes anything cooked there in any way. The exact words chosen set the reach of the vow.

keyTerms.meaning: Its boiling, meaning food boiled in the pot
Whatever goes down into a pot

steps.whatToRemember: Throughout the משנה, the vow covers exactly what the person's words mean in normal speech, nothing more.

phrases.english: One who vows off food made in a pot
is forbidden only food boiled in it,
If he said: "Whatever goes down into a pot is konam for me, that I will not taste"
he is forbidden everything cooked in a pot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of vow wordings, now about pot food
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מעשה קדרה covers only boiled food; היורד לקדרה covers everything cooked in a pot.

steps.title: רבי יאשיה forbids roasted food, with a hint from a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records that רבי יאשיה forbids roasted food to one who vowed off cooked food, hinting to this from the קרבן פסח being called 'cooked.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי יאשיה forbids roasted food. Even though there is no real proof, there is a hint, since the פסוק says, 'They cooked the פסח in fire according to the law.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי יאשיה disagrees with the first ruling of the משנה and says roasted food is included in a vow on cooked food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קרבן פסח must be roasted, yet the פסוק calls it 'cooked.' That shows roasting can be called cooking. רבי יאשיה admits this is only a זכר (hint), not a full proof.

keyTerms.meaning: A hint or allusion to the idea

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יאשיה is arguing on the very first line of the משנה (step 1), not on the later pot cases.

phrases.english: Gemara: It was taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Yoshiya forbids,
phrases.notes: He forbids roasted food to someone who vowed off cooked food.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לְדָבָר
phrases.english: and although there is no proof for the matter,
there is a hint to the matter,
as it says: "And they cooked the Pesach offering in fire according to the law."
phrases.notes: דברי הימים ב 35:13. The פסח is roasted, yet the פסוק calls it 'cooked.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an opposing opinion to the משנה's first ruling
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יאשיה, a vow on cooked food also forbids roasted food.

steps.title: Suggesting the argument is Torah language versus people's language
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that רבי יאשיה follows לשון תורה while our תנא follows לשון בני אדם in נדרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this is their argument? רבי יאשיה holds that we follow the Torah's language, and our תנא holds that in vows we follow the way people talk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to identify the root of the disagreement. It suggests that the two sides argue about a general rule for reading vows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the Torah calls roasting 'cooking,' following Torah language would forbid roasted food, as רבי יאשיה says. Following people's speech would permit it, as the משנה says. The word לימא signals that this is only a suggestion, and the next step will test it.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (a suggestion that is often rejected)
The Torah's way of using words
The way ordinary people use words
Our תנא, the author of our משנה

phrases.english: Shall we say they disagree about this,
that Rabbi Yoshiya holds:
follow the language of the Torah,
and our tanna holds:

phrases.aramaic: בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם?
phrases.english: with vows, follow the language of people?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to explain the root of the argument between step 1 and step 4
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the dispute about whether נדרים follow לשון תורה or לשון בני אדם?

steps.title: Everyone follows people's language; local speech differed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion: all agree נדרים follow לשון בני אדם, but in רבי יאשיה's area people called roasted food 'cooked.'
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees that in vows we follow the way people talk. Each Sage ruled based on his own place. Where our תנא lived, roasted was called roasted and cooked was called cooked. Where רבי יאשיה lived, even roasted food was called cooked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion and says the two Sages do not argue about the rule at all. They only describe how people spoke in different places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general principle is shared by both: a vow means what people mean by their words. The difference in ruling comes from real local speech. This means רבי יאשיה's real reason must be how people in his area talked, not the פסוק. The next step challenges exactly this point.

keyTerms.meaning: Each Sage according to his own place

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that בנדרים הלך אחר לשון בני אדם. Their different rulings come from different local ways of speaking, not from different principles.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a נדר is judged by the speaker's own community's language. The same words can mean different things in different places.

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees

phrases.aramaic: בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם,
phrases.english: that with vows we follow the language of people,

phrases.aramaic: מָר כִּי אַתְרֵיהּ וּמָר כִּי אַתְרֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and this Sage ruled by his place, and that Sage ruled by his place.
In the place of our tanna,
roasted food they call roasted,
and cooked food they call cooked.
In the place of Rabbi Yoshiya,
even roasted food they call cooked.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion in step 5 and offers a different explanation of the dispute
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the Sages argue over לשון תורה versus לשון בני אדם
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The rulings can be explained by different local speech habits while both sides share the same principle

steps.title: But רבי יאשיה quoted a verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges Step 6: if רבי יאשיה brings a פסוק, he seems to be following the Torah's language, not how people speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he brings a verse for it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from Step 6. It points out that רבי יאשיה actually quoted a פסוק (the קרבן פסח called 'cooked').
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said everyone agrees that vows follow לשון בני אדם, and that רבי יאשיה was only describing how people in his area talked. But if he relied on a פסוק, it looks like his reason comes from לשון תורה after all. That would bring back the suggestion from Step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: He takes it, meaning he brings it as his source

phrases.english: But he brings a verse for it!
phrases.notes: The verse is the one about the קרבן פסח being called 'cooked' (Step 4).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in Step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יאשיה also follows לשון בני אדם
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Bringing a פסוק as a source suggests his ruling is based on Torah language, not on how people speak.

steps.title: The verse is only a hint
steps.stepSummary: The verse is just an אסמכתא, a support, and not the real source of רבי יאשיה's ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק is only a hint that leans on the ruling. It is not the true reason for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יאשיה's real reason is still how people in his area spoke. The פסוק is added only as a nice support, which fits his own wording in the ברייתא, where it was called just a hint (זכר לדבר). So the answer from Step 6 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A verse used as a hint or support, not as the real source of a law

steps.whyThisMatters: This finishes the רבי יאשיה discussion: all opinions agree that vows follow לשון בני אדם.

phrases.english: It is merely a support.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Downgrading the source: the verse is only a hint, not the basis
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse is רבי יאשיה's real source, so he follows לשון תורה
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse is only an אסמכתא; his ruling is based on local speech

steps.title: Why is a thick dish allowed?
steps.stepSummary: Going back to the משנה, the גמרא asks: he vowed off 'תבשיל', so why may he eat a thick cooked dish?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'קונם a cooked dish,' and so on. But he vowed off cooked food!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the line of the משנה from Step 2 and questions it. A thick dish is also cooked, so why is it permitted?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ruled that someone who vowed off 'תבשיל' may still eat thick pot dishes. But a thick dish is cooked too, so the vow seems to cover it. The גמרא wants to know what makes it fall outside the word 'תבשיל'.

keyTerms.meaning: A vow word meaning 'forbidden to me like a קרבן'

phrases.english: 'Konam a cooked dish,' and so on.
But he vowed off cooked food!

steps.triggerLanguage: קֻוֽנָּם תַּבְשִׁיל כּוּ׳. וְהָא מִתַּבְשִׁיל נְדַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the רבי יאשיה side discussion and returns to the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a thick dish is permitted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A thick dish is cooked, so a vow on 'cooked food' should include it.

steps.title: אביי: 'תבשיל' means food eaten with bread
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that this תנא calls 'תבשיל' only something eaten together with bread; a thick dish is eaten alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: This תנא calls anything that bread is eaten with 'a cooked dish.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question from Step 9 by defining the word 'תבשיל' the way this תנא uses it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For this תנא, 'תבשיל' means a dish you eat alongside bread, like a side dish or dip. A thick dish is eaten by itself, not with bread, so it is not called 'תבשיל' and the vow does not cover it.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה teacher whose wording is being explained

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the word in a vow is defined by how it is used in real speech, not by the cooking method.

phrases.english: Abaye said: This tanna
anything with which bread is eaten —
they call it a cooked dish.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הַאי תַּנָּא כֹּל מִידֵּי דְּמִתְאֲכֵל בֵּיהּ רִיפְתָּא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'תבשיל' means anything cooked, including thick dishes
steps.terutzMaskana: 'תבשיל' means a dish eaten with bread, so a thick dish is excluded

steps.title: A ברייתא supports אביי
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא forbids soft gourds 'that the sick eat their bread with', which shows that 'תבשיל' means food eaten with bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so a ברייתא teaches: One who vows off cooked food is forbidden in all kinds of cooked food: roasted, boiled and cooked. He is also forbidden in soft gourds, which sick people eat with their bread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up אביי's definition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives a reason why soft gourds count as 'תבשיל': sick people eat their bread with them. That reason only makes sense if 'תבשיל' means something eaten together with bread, which is exactly אביי's point.

phrases.english: And so it is taught: One who vows off cooked food —
is forbidden in all kinds of cooked food,
and is forbidden in roasted, well-boiled and cooked food,
and is forbidden in soft gourds
with which the sick eat their bread.

steps.raayaObject: אביי's rule that 'תבשיל' means food eaten with bread
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that includes soft gourds because the sick eat their bread with them

steps.title: Do sick people really eat gourds?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא with the story of a doctor who left רבי ירמיה's house when he saw a gourd there, calling it an 'angel of death' for a sick person.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? Once רבי ירמיה was sick, and a doctor came to heal him. He saw a gourd lying in the house, left him and walked out. He said: This man has the angel of death in his house, and I should go in to heal him?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the ברייתא's claim that sick people eat gourds by telling a story that shows gourds are dangerous for the sick. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said sick people eat their bread with soft gourds. But the doctor treated a gourd in a sick man's house as so harmful that he refused to treat him. So how can the ברייתא describe gourds as normal food for the sick?
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up קְרָא (a verse) from Step 7 with קַרָא (a gourd) here. They are spelled almost the same but mean very different things.

phrases.english: Is that so?!
phrases.notes: He is asking: do sick people really eat gourds, as the ברייתא said?

phrases.english: But Rabbi Yirmeya fell ill,
a certain doctor came in to him to heal him,
he saw a gourd that was lying in his house,
he left him and went out.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: מַלְאַךְ מוֹתָא אִית לֵיהּ לְדֵין בְּבֵיתֵיהּ,
phrases.english: He said: This one has the angel of death in his house,
and I should go in to heal him?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges a detail of the ברייתא brought as support in Step 11
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's statement that sick people eat their bread with gourds
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A doctor's reaction shows gourds are deadly for the sick, so sick people would not eat them.

steps.title: Soft gourds versus hard gourds
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about soft gourds, which help the sick. The doctor was talking about hard gourds, which harm them.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not a contradiction: this one is about soft gourds, and that one is about hard gourds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction from Step 12 by saying the two sources are talking about different kinds of gourds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא itself said 'soft gourds,' so those are good for a sick person. The doctor in רבי ירמיה's house must have seen hard gourds, which are dangerous for the sick. Once each source is about a different gourd, the sources no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. The opening of an answer that removes a contradiction.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
This one is about soft gourds,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the ברייתא, which forbade soft gourds as a תבשיל.

phrases.english: that one is about hard gourds.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא — בְּרַכִּיכֵי, הָא — בְּאַשּׁוּנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 12 by splitting the cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): different types of gourd
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every gourd is the same, so it cannot be both good and deadly for the sick.
steps.terutzMaskana: Soft gourds help the sick; hard gourds harm them.

steps.title: The gourd itself versus its inside
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר עולא gives a different answer: the doctor meant the whole gourd, while the ברייתא meant the soft inside of the gourd.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר עולא said: This one is about the gourd itself, and that one is about the inside of the gourd.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר עולא offers a second way to solve the same contradiction, this time by splitting between parts of the gourd.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The doctor's warning was about eating the gourd itself, which harms a sick person. The ברייתא, which says the sick eat their bread with gourds, is about the soft inside of the gourd. Same plant, different part, so there is no contradiction.

phrases.english: Rava bar Ulla said:
This one is about the gourd itself,
phrases.notes: This is the doctor's story, where the gourd was called an 'angel of death.'

phrases.english: and that one is about the inside of the gourd.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא בַּר עוּלָּא אָמַר: הָא — בְּקַרָא גּוּפֵיהּ, וְהָא — בְּגַוֵּויהּ דִּקְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to Step 12's קשיא, different from Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by part of the food
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources are talking about the same food.
steps.terutzMaskana: The whole gourd is harmful; its inside is good to eat with bread.

steps.title: רב יהודה shows the inside of a gourd is eaten with other food
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה's statement shows that people eat the inside of a gourd as a side dish, supporting רבא בר עולא. He adds that the flax tip is eaten with כותחא, but this should not be told to an עם הארץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יהודה said: The inside of a gourd is eaten with chard; the inside of flax is eaten with כותחא. And this matter may not be said in front of an עם הארץ.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב יהודה to back up רבא בר עולא: the inside of a gourd really is a known food that goes together with something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא בר עולא needed to show that the inside of a gourd is a real, healthy food eaten alongside other things. רב יהודה confirms this by giving the best way to eat it. His extra line about not telling an עם הארץ refers to the flax: if ignorant people knew it was tasty, they might uproot flax to eat it and ruin the crop.

keyTerms.meaning: The inner part (or soft tip) of a plant.
כותחא, a dip made from bread crumbs and sour milk.

phrases.english: As Rav Yehuda said:
The inside of the gourd goes with chard,
the inside of flax goes with kutach.
And this matter is forbidden
to say in front of an ignorant person.
phrases.notes: The worry is that he would pull up flax plants to eat them and destroy the crop.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: לוּלִיבָּא דְקַרָא בְּסִילְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא בר עולא's answer in Step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That the inside of a gourd is a normal food eaten together with something else.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The statement of רב יהודה about how to eat the inside of a gourd and of flax.

steps.title: The 'sick' in the ברייתא are the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a third answer: the 'sick' in the ברייתא are Torah scholars who are weak from learning, not truly sick people.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Who are the 'sick'? The רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא solves the contradiction a third way, by reading the word 'sick' in the ברייתא differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The doctor was right that gourds harm people who are really sick. But the ברייתא's 'sick' are the רבנן, who are weak from toiling in Torah, and for them gourds are good. Now the two sources describe different people.
steps.confusionAlert: רבא does not mean the רבנן are actually ill. He means they are weak like sick people, so gourds suit them.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Who are the 'sick'? The Sages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to Step 12, different from Steps 13 and 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading a word in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Sick' in the ברייתא means truly ill people, like in the doctor story.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Sick' means weakened Torah scholars, for whom gourds are good.
steps.whatToRemember: Three answers to one contradiction: (1) soft vs. hard gourds, (2) the gourd itself vs. its inside, (3) truly sick people vs. weakened רבנן.

steps.title: רבא is consistent with his own view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to show that רבא's answer matches another statement of his. The statement itself comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא follows his own reasoning, as רבא said:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line: the גמרא is about to quote another statement of רבא that fits his idea that the רבנן are like sick people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'רבא לטעמיה' tells us that רבא's answer is not a one-time idea. He says something similar elsewhere. The actual statement continues in the next part of the גמרא.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning; consistent with what he says elsewhere.

phrases.english: Rava follows his own reasoning,
as Rava said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets up support for רבא's answer in Step 16.
steps.raayaObject: That רבא really holds the רבנן are like sick people.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Another statement of רבא, quoted in the next section.
